claims.text: Premelting and melting of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetically restricted, stochastic nucleation of local liquid regions.
Limited atomic mobility in a solid precursor can produce nanoscale compositional fluctuations or local segregation.
Limited atomic mobility produces lattice strain in these Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations and lattice strains lower local melting points.
Local inhomogeneities cause melting to be gradual and spatially heterogeneous.
Simpler binary-alloy nanoparticles melt more abruptly than the proposed Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase solids with a homogeneous average composition.
A chemically mixed five-element nanoparticle can nevertheless exhibit local segregation when atomic mobility is limited.
Reduction of a solid mixed precursor at moderate temperature limits free atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy itself contributes to limited atomic mobility in the solid nanoparticles.
Some nanoparticle regions premelt below the bulk melting point.
With increasing temperature, isolated liquid domains coalesce into a fully molten particle.
The stochastic spatial distribution of local compositions and defects controls the heterogeneous melting trajectory.
In-situ heating will reveal localized liquid spots or loss of crystallinity before complete melting.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting-temperature interval than similarly sized binary-alloy nanoparticles.
Binary or simpler multicomponent nanoparticles have higher atomic mobility and a relatively sharp melting point.
The proposed melting mechanism applies primarily to nanoparticles synthesized under conditions that restrict atomic rearrangement.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to liquid-phase or other synthesis routes that permit extensive atomic rearrangement.
A similarly sized binary-alloy nanoparticle is the control for comparing transition width and spatial uniformity of melting.
A sharp, spatially uniform transition near the bulk melting point, with no local premelting at any tested heating rate, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
